description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a majestic dish, a true masterpiece of Mexican cuisine with layers of profound flavor. This dark, rich sauce combines an incredible array of chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and chocolate, simmered to perfection. It is a celebratory dish that embodies the heart and soul of Oaxaca.

instructions.title: Prepare and Toast Chiles
instructions.text: Carefully wipe the dried chiles clean. Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Toast the chiles for 30-60 seconds per side until fragrant but not burnt. Be careful not to burn them or the mole will be bitter. Remove from heat, place in a bowl, cover with hot water, and let soak for at least 30 minutes until softened. Drain and reserve the soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Roast Aromatics and Toast Spices
instructions.text: In the same skillet, roast the tomatillos, tomatoes, onion, and garlic until lightly charred and softened, about 8-10 minutes. Set aside. In a separate dry skillet, lightly toast the almonds, pecans, pumpkin seeds, and sesame seeds until fragrant. Separately, toast the raisins, dried plantain, and stale bread until lightly golden. Toast the cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, and cumin seeds until aromatic.

instructions.title: First Blend - Chiles and Aromatics
instructions.text: In a blender, combine the softened chiles with the roasted tomatillos, tomatoes, onion, and garlic. Add 1-2 cups of chicken broth. Blend until a smooth paste forms, adding more broth if needed. Strain this mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl, pressing hard on the solids to extract all liquid. Discard the solids. This step is crucial for a smooth mole.

instructions.title: Second Blend - Nuts, Seeds, and Spices
instructions.text: In the blender, combine all the toasted nuts, seeds, raisins, dried plantain, bread, and toasted whole spices (cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, cumin). Add the dried Mexican oregano and thyme. Add 1-2 cups of chicken broth and blend until a very smooth paste. This may take a few minutes of blending, scraping down the sides as needed. Strain this mixture through the same fine-mesh sieve into the bowl with the chile paste, pressing hard.

instructions.title: Cook the Mole Base
instructions.text: Heat the lard or oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Once hot, carefully pour in the combined strained mole paste. It will splatter, so be careful. Stir constantly for 15-20 minutes until the mole darkens significantly and thickens, reducing in volume by about a third. This step is essential to deepen the flavor and cook out any raw taste.

instructions.title: Simmer and Finish the Mole
instructions.text: Gradually add the remaining chicken broth to the mole paste, stirring constantly to incorporate. Bring to a simmer. Add the chopped Mexican chocolate and stir until it completely melts and is incorporated. Reduce heat to low, cover partially, and simmer for at least 1 to 1.5 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The mole should be rich, dark, and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Season with salt and a pinch of sugar if needed to balance the flavors.

instructions.title: Serve Your Oaxacan Black Mole
instructions.text: Once the mole has simmered to perfection, add your cooked chicken or turkey pieces directly into the sauce to warm through, or serve the mole generously over the chicken. Garnish with toasted sesame seeds and serve alongside warm white rice. Enjoy this authentic taste of Oaxaca!

tips: Always toast your chiles and spices carefully; burning them will result in a bitter mole. A light toast is all you need to release their aromatics.
For the smoothest mole, straining the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve is crucial. You can use the back of a spoon to push the paste through.
Mole Negro tastes even better the next day as the flavors deepen and meld. Make it ahead of time and gently reheat, adding a little broth if it's too thick.
article:
Embark on a culinary journey to the heart of Oaxaca, Mexico, where ancient traditions and vibrant flavors converge to create one of the world's most complex and revered sauces: Mole Negro. More than just a dish, Mole Negro is a celebration, a symphony of ingredients that tells a story of heritage, patience, and profound flavor. It’s a sauce that demands respect and rewards effort, transforming humble poultry into an unforgettable feast. If you’ve ever dreamed of recreating the magic of authentic Mexican dinner recipes in your own kitchen, preparing this iconic Oaxacan Black Mole is an experience you won't want to miss.

## What is Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro)?

Oaxacan Black Mole, or Mole Negro, stands as the king among Oaxaca's "seven moles," renowned for its astonishing depth and dark, almost black hue. It's a culinary masterpiece that can feature upwards of 30 ingredients, meticulously toasted, ground, and simmered to perfection. Unlike simpler sauces, Mole Negro is a dance between smoky, sweet, spicy, earthy, and even slightly bitter notes, creating an intricate flavor profile that evolves with every bite. Its characteristic color comes from the careful charring of a specific blend of chiles—primarily chilhuacle, mulato, and pasilla Oaxaca—alongside nuts, seeds, and Mexican chocolate. Traditionally reserved for special occasions like weddings, baptisms, and major holidays, preparing this Oaxacan Black Mole is an act of love and a testament to the rich culinary heritage of the region. It’s not just food; it’s an edible piece of Oaxacan culture.

## Ingredients for Authentic Oaxacan Black Mole

The complexity of Oaxacan Black Mole begins with its extensive ingredient list. While some chiles can be challenging to find outside Mexico, a dedicated search at a well-stocked Mexican grocery store will yield the best results.

**The Chiles (the heart of the mole):**
*   **Ancho Chiles:** Dried poblano, offering fruity, smoky notes.
*   **Mulato Chiles:** Darker, with chocolate, licorice, and cherry undertones.
*   **Pasilla Chiles:** Long, slender, with prune-like, earthy flavors.
*   **Chipotle Chiles (optional, for heat):** Smoked jalapeños, adding a fiery kick.
*   *(For truly authentic flavor, seek out Chilhuacle Negro, Chilcostle, and Tostado chiles if possible.)*

**Aromatics & Vegetables:**
*   White onion, garlic cloves
*   Ripe tomatoes, tomatillos

**Spices (a carefully balanced blend):**
*   Cinnamon stick, whole cloves, black peppercorns, cumin seeds, coriander seeds, allspice berries, star anise (optional), dried oregano, dried thyme.

**Thickeners & Body Builders (for texture and richness):**
*   Stale tortillas, day-old bread (like a bolillo or telera)
*   Raw almonds, raw peanuts, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), sesame seeds
*   Plantain (ripe, for sweetness and body)
*   Raisins (for fruity sweetness)

**Sweeteners & Darkeners:**
*   Mexican chocolate (bitter, typically with cinnamon and almond notes)
*   Piloncillo (Mexican unrefined brown sugar cone) or dark brown sugar

**Fats & Liquids:**
*   Lard or vegetable oil (for frying)
*   Rich chicken broth

**Seasoning:**
*   Salt to taste

## Step-by-Step Guide to Making Mole Negro

Patience is your most important ingredient when making this Oaxacan Black Mole. Break it down into manageable stages, and enjoy the process!

1.  **Prepare the Chiles:** Carefully remove stems and seeds from all chiles. Lightly toast them in a dry pan over medium heat for 30 seconds to 1 minute per side until fragrant (be careful not to burn, or they'll turn bitter). Immediately transfer to a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for 20-30 minutes until soft. Drain, reserving some of the soaking liquid.
2.  **Toast & Fry Aromatics & Thickeners:** In a large skillet or Dutch oven with a bit of lard or oil, fry the onion and garlic until softened. Remove. Then, in batches, fry the tomatoes and tomatillos until charred. Next, toast the spices (cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, etc.) until fragrant. Finally, fry the almonds, peanuts, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, tortillas, bread, plantain, and raisins until lightly golden. Keep everything separate initially, as they cook at different rates.
3.  **Blend in Batches:** Combine the rehydrated chiles, fried aromatics (onion, garlic, tomatoes, tomatillos), toasted spices, and fried nuts, seeds, bread, plantain, and raisins in a high-speed blender. Add some chicken broth and a little chile soaking liquid to help it blend. Process until as smooth as possible. You’ll likely need to do this in several batches.
4.  **Strain for Silkiness:** For the most authentic, silky texture, press the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl, using a spatula to push the pulp through. Discard any remaining solids. This step is laborious but highly recommended for a truly refined Oaxacan Black Mole.
5.  **Simmer the Mole:** Heat a generous amount of lard or oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Carefully pour in the strained mole paste (it will splatter!). Stir constantly for 15-20 minutes until the mole darkens significantly and thickens, developing a rich aroma. This frying step is crucial for developing deep flavor.
6.  **Add Remaining Ingredients & Simmer:** Gradually stir in the remaining chicken broth, Mexican chocolate, and piloncillo (or brown sugar). Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, stirring occasionally, for at least 1 to 2 hours, or even longer. The mole should thicken further and its flavors will meld and deepen. Add more broth if it becomes too thick.
7.  **Season and Serve:** Taste and adjust seasoning with salt. The mole should be a balance of sweet, spicy, and earthy.

## Pro Tips for the Best Oaxacan Black Mole

*   **Source Quality Chiles:** This is non-negotiable. Visit a Mexican market for the best selection of dried chiles.
*   **Don't Burn the Chiles:** A quick toast enhances flavor; burning them will make your mole bitter. Watch them closely!
*   **Patience is Key:** This isn't a weeknight meal. Dedicate a good chunk of time to the process. The long simmer is essential for flavor development.
*   **Taste and Adjust:** Mole is about balance. Continuously taste and adjust for sweetness, spice, and saltiness. A little more chocolate or piloncillo can balance heat, while a pinch of salt can brighten all flavors.
*   **Make Ahead:** Oaxacan Black Mole often tastes even better the next day, after the flavors have had more time to meld.
*   **Freeze It:** Mole freezes beautifully for up to several months. Make a large batch and enjoy it later!

## Serving Suggestions for Mole Negro

Traditionally, Oaxacan Black Mole is served with poultry. Poached or roasted chicken pieces are the most classic accompaniment, allowing the rich sauce to truly shine.

*   **Classic Chicken Mole:** Ladle generously over shredded or whole pieces of cooked chicken (or turkey). Serve with warm corn tortillas and fluffy white rice to soak up every drop of the exquisite sauce.
*   **Enchiladas de Mole:** Fill corn tortillas with shredded chicken, roll them, and smother them in warm Mole Negro, perhaps topped with a sprinkle of sesame seeds and a drizzle of Mexican crema or crumbled queso fresco.
*   **Tamales:** Use the mole as a filling for tamales, often combined with chicken.
*   **Tacos or Sopes:** A dollop of mole over grilled meat in a warm tortilla or a thick masa sope makes for a gourmet bite.
*   **Vegetarian Options:** Serve over roasted sweet potatoes, grilled portobello mushrooms, or hearty black bean cakes.

## Variations & Substitutions for Your Mole Negro

While authenticity is wonderful, don't be afraid to adapt this Oaxacan Black Mole to your pantry and preferences.

*   **Chile Substitutions:** If specific Oaxacan chiles are unavailable, you can increase the amounts of ancho, mulato, and pasilla chiles. A small amount of chipotle can add a smoky heat.
*   **Nut/Seed Variety:** Feel free to adjust the mix of almonds, peanuts, and pumpkin seeds based on what you have. Pecans can also be a delicious addition.
*   **Sweeteners:** Dark brown sugar can be used in place of piloncillo.
*   **Vegetarian/Vegan Mole:** Substitute chicken broth with a high-quality vegetable broth. For serving, use roasted vegetables, plantains, or tofu instead of poultry. Ensure your chocolate is dairy-free.
*   **Spice Adjustments:** Feel free to tweak the spice blend to your liking. If you don't have allspice or star anise, for example, it won't ruin the dish, though the flavor profile will subtly shift.

Creating Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary adventure, a journey into the heart of Mexican gastronomy. It's a dish that connects you to generations of cooks and celebrates the incredible bounty of flavors found in Oaxaca. While it requires time and dedication, the reward—a deeply complex, utterly delicious sauce that will impress anyone lucky enough to taste it—is immeasurable. So gather your ingredients, clear your schedule, and prepare to create a truly unforgettable Mexican dinner recipe.
